clinicalPearls: Chronic tophaceous gout is the advanced stage in which longstanding, poorly controlled hyperuricaemia leads to visible or palpable deposits of monosodium urate (tophi) in and around joints and soft tissues
Tophi commonly form over the first metatarsophalangeal joint, the fingers, the olecranon bursa, the Achilles tendon, and the helix of the ear, and may ulcerate to discharge chalky white material
The condition reflects a large total-body urate burden and usually indicates years of untreated or undertreated gout
Tophi cause joint-destroying erosions, deformity, chronic pain, and reduced function, and can restrict movement or entrap nerves
Radiographs show characteristic well-defined 'punched-out' erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges, with joint space relatively preserved until late
Aspiration or biopsy of a tophus reveals abundant needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals

The cornerstone of management is long-term urate-lowering therapy to a low target (treat-to-target), which over time dissolves tophi and prevents further damage; it is not started or stopped during an acute flare and is continued through flares
reference.pathophysiology: Prolonged hyperuricaemia produces a large body burden of monosodium urate that precipitates as aggregated crystal masses (tophi) surrounded by a chronic granulomatous, foreign-body inflammatory reaction. Tophi within and around joints erode bone and cartilage, generating the characteristic punched-out erosions and progressive structural damage, while in soft tissues they form firm nodules that may ulcerate and discharge. Sustained lowering of the serum urate below the saturation point reverses the process by allowing the crystals to dissolve gradually.
additionalDifferentials: Osteoarthritis with Heberden and Bouchard nodes
additionalInvestigations: Aspiration or biopsy of a tophus or joint with polarised microscopy for negatively birefringent urate crystals
Serum urate to guide and monitor treat-to-target therapy
Radiographs for punched-out erosions with overhanging edges
Dual-energy CT to quantify and map urate deposits
Ultrasound for tophi and the double-contour sign
Renal function and assessment of cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidity
Swab or culture if an ulcerated tophus raises suspicion of secondary infection
redFlags: An ulcerated or discharging tophus with possible secondary infection
Nerve compression caused by a tophaceous mass
Coexistent septic arthritis in a chronically damaged joint
Significant renal impairment influencing the choice of therapy
reference.prognosis: With sustained urate-lowering therapy to target, tophi gradually resolve, attacks stop, and further joint damage is prevented; established erosions and deformity may nonetheless be permanent, and poor adherence leads to ongoing destruction and disability.
pitfalls: Failing to commit to long-term treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy
Stopping urate-lowering therapy once tophi shrink, allowing recurrence
Starting or stopping urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare
Missing secondary infection of an ulcerated tophus
Attributing the deformity to another arthropathy without confirming urate crystals
management: Long-term urate-lowering therapy with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor such as allopurinol or febuxostat, titrated treat-to-target to dissolve tophi
Add a uricosuric such as probenecid, or consider pegloticase, for refractory disease or intolerance of xanthine oxidase inhibitors
Anti-inflammatory flare prophylaxis with colchicine or an NSAID when starting urate-lowering therapy to prevent mobilisation flares
Treat acute flares with an NSAID, colchicine, or corticosteroids
Lifestyle measures including reduced alcohol and purine-rich food intake, weight loss, and review of urate-raising drugs such as diuretics
Address concurrent cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic comorbidity
Refer for surgical debulking of tophi that ulcerate, become infected, entrap nerves, or impair joint function
Monitor serum urate to confirm sustained suppression below the crystal-saturation point
